2642.trap_explanation: Nitroglycerine sounds like it could be derived from coal chemistry but it cannot — it requires nitration of glycerol (a by-product of biodiesel/soap), not syngas. Ethanol (syngas fermentation/catalysis) and urea (syngas → ammonia → urea via Haber-Bosch) are both genuine coal gasification products. Official answer is (c) all three; note nitroglycerine pathway is contested. DATA-QUALITY FLAG.

statements.text: Ethanol
statements.reason: Syngas (CO + H2) from coal gasification can be catalytically converted to ethanol via Fischer-Tropsch-type synthesis or fermentation. Industrial pathway confirmed.

statements.text: Nitroglycerine
statements.reason: Per official UPSC answer (c). The accepted pathway: syngas → methanol → glycerol → nitroglycerine via nitration. A multi-step indirect route, not a direct product. Controversial in practice.

statements.text: Urea
statements.reason: Syngas from coal gasification → ammonia via Haber-Bosch (H2 + N2) → urea (ammonia + CO2). Texas Clean Energy Project is a real-world example of coal-to-urea production.

answer_justification.fact: Official answer: all three producible via coal gasification → option (c). Ethanol and urea pathways are direct; nitroglycerine is indirect via syngas→glycerol chain.
answer_justification.elimination_path: Ethanol (syngas catalysis — clear). Urea (Haber-Bosch from syngas H2 — clear). Nitroglycerine: official answer accepts it via multi-step syngas→glycerol→nitration route → (c).

2654.trap_explanation: Three 'NO virus can...' absolutes — all false. Viruses are the most abundant entities in ocean water (~10 million/mL). Bacteriophages infect bacteria by definition. Many viruses (e.g., adenoviruses, herpesviruses) alter host cell transcription machinery. Every statement uses an impossible universal negative.

statements.text: No virus can survive in ocean waters.
statements.reason: Oceans contain ~10 million viruses per mL of seawater. Marine viruses (bacteriophages, algae viruses) are the most abundant biological entities on Earth and drive biogeochemical cycles.

statements.text: No virus can infect bacteria.
statements.reason: Bacteriophages (phages) are viruses that specifically infect bacteria. They are among the most extensively studied viruses; T4 phage infecting E. coli is a canonical example.

statements.text: No virus can change the cellular transcriptional activity in host cells.
statements.reason: Many viruses hijack host transcription: adenoviruses use host RNA polymerase II; herpes viruses redirect transcription; HIV integrates into host genome and drives viral gene expression.

answer_justification.fact: All three statements use false universal negatives — each has well-known counterexamples → option (d) None correct.
answer_justification.elimination_path: I: ocean teems with viruses (10M/mL) — false. II: bacteriophages infect bacteria by definition — false. III: adenoviruses/herpesviruses alter host transcription — false. All wrong → (d).

2700.trap_explanation: HMX and CL-20 could be confused with rocket fuels or propellants because they are high-energy materials. The distinction: high-energy explosives (detonation-based) vs high-energy fuels (deflagration/combustion-based). All three are detonation explosives used in warheads, not propellants or refrigerants.

distractor_analysis.reason: HFO alternatives are chemical refrigerants (HFCs, HFOs). CL-20/HMX/LLM-105 are explosives with no refrigerant chemistry.
Cruise missile fuels (kerosene-based) are combustion fuels. These compounds are detonation explosives — different energy release mechanism.
Rocket propellants (HTPB, AP-based) deflagrate. CL-20/HMX/LLM-105 are secondary explosives that detonate. Distinct category.

answer_justification.fact: CL-20 (hexanitrohexaazaisowurtzitane), HMX, and LLM-105 are all high-energy explosives used in military munitions and warheads.
answer_justification.hook: CL-20 was developed at China Lake Naval Station; LLM-105 at Lawrence Livermore — both are insensitive yet powerful warhead explosives.
answer_justification.elimination_path: Not refrigerants (a) — wrong domain entirely. Not cruise missile fuel (c) — fuel ≠ explosive. Not rocket propellant (d) — propellants deflagrate, these detonate. → (b).

972.trap_explanation: All three bodies coordinate national policy — they look alike functionally. The trap is conflating 'constitutional authority exists' with 'constitutionally established.' ISC is the only one where the Constitution itself empowers and authorises its creation (Article 263); the others come from statute or executive order.

statements.text: The Inter-State Council
statements.reason: Article 263 of the Constitution empowers the President to establish an Inter-State Council. Its creation derives directly from a constitutional provision — established 1990 by presidential order under Article 263.

statements.text: The National Security Council
statements.reason: NSC was created by a Cabinet Resolution (executive order) in November 1998 under PM Vajpayee. No constitutional article or Act of Parliament establishes it.

statements.text: Zonal Councils
statements.reason: Zonal Councils were set up by the States Reorganisation Act, 1956 — a statutory body, not a constitutional one. No article in the Constitution mandates or establishes them.

answer_justification.fact: Only ISC (Article 263) qualifies — NSC is executive, Zonal Councils are statutory → option (a) Only one.
answer_justification.elimination_path: Eliminate NSC immediately (1998 Cabinet Resolution, no Act, no article). Eliminate Zonal Councils (States Reorganisation Act 1956, statutory). Only ISC has a constitutional article → (a).

974.trap_explanation: Statements I, II, and IV each contain a single inverted or swapped claim. I swaps territorial scope (excludes overseas, but Act includes them). II swaps 'only CJI' for 'CJI or SC judge or eminent person.' IV inverts the PM inquiry rule entirely — Lokpal can inquire, with conditions. Only III states the Act verbatim.

statements.text: The power of Lokpal applies to public servants of India, but not to the Indian public servants posted outside India.
statements.reason: Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act 2013 explicitly covers public servants 'in and outside India.' The exclusion of overseas postings is a direct inversion of the Act's text.

statements.reason: The 'only CJI' claim is the inversion. The Act allows Chairperson to be CJI/former CJI OR a Judge/former Judge of Supreme Court OR an eminent person meeting specified criteria.

answer_justification.fact: Only III is true (age 45 minimum) — I, II, IV each contain a direct inversion → option (a) III only.
answer_justification.elimination_path: Identify the inversion in each: I (overseas excluded — wrong, Act covers them), II (only CJI — wrong, eminent persons qualify too), IV (cannot inquire — wrong, can with conditions). III survives as the only verbatim-correct statement → (a).

81.trap_explanation: All four regions are mahajanapadas (correct concept) but two pairs swap the river — this is the classic 'right concept, wrong geography' trap. Kamboja is the NW frontier (Afghanistan/Hindu Kush), nowhere near Vipas (Beas) which flows through Punjab. Avanti is Malwa/Ujjain on the Sipra; Mahanadi flows through Odisha — completely different region.

pairs.reason: Asmaka mahajanapada lay in modern Maharashtra/N Karnataka along the Godavari, capital at Potana/Paithan.
Kamboja was the NW frontier mahajanapada (Hindu Kush region, around Rajapura). Vipas is the Beas, which flows through Punjab — far east of Kamboja territory.
Avanti was Malwa region with capital Ujjain on the Sipra (and southern capital Mahishmati on the Narmada). Mahanadi flows through Odisha — entirely different region.
Kosala's capital Ayodhya/Saketa lay on the Sarayu (Ghaghara) river in present-day Uttar Pradesh.

answer_justification.elimination_path: Eliminate any option that requires Kamboja in Punjab (II) or Avanti in Odisha (III) — both geographically impossible. Two correct pairs remain → (b).

2285.trap_explanation: Both reasons (II and III) are independently true AND each provides a distinct causal pathway by which circular economy reduces GHG emissions. This is the rare 'both correct and both explain' answer (a) — students often hesitate, looking for partial-truth or single-explanation patterns that aren't there.

claim_statement.text: Circular economy reduces the emissions of greenhouse gases.
claim_statement.reason: Established in IPCC and UNEP literature: circular models cut lifecycle GHG by reducing extraction, processing, and disposal emissions.

supporting_statements.text: Circular economy reduces the use of raw materials as inputs.
supporting_statements.reason: True (definitional). Reduced raw material use → less mining/extraction → less energy use upstream → less GHG. Direct explanatory link to claim.

supporting_statements.text: Circular economy reduces wastage in the production process.
supporting_statements.reason: True (definitional). Less wastage → less material processed for the same output → less manufacturing energy → less GHG. Independent explanatory link.

answer_justification.fact: Both II and III are true AND each independently explains why circular economy cuts GHG → option (a).
answer_justification.elimination_path: Verify II (raw material reduction → upstream extraction GHG cut). Verify III (wastage reduction → manufacturing GHG cut). Both link to claim independently — neither relies on the other. So (a), not (b).

607.trap_explanation: Ambedkar is the most famous anti-caste reformer in modern Indian history, so option B feels right by association. The trap is recognising that the SPECIFIC movement asked about — Self-Respect Movement — was a Tamil Nadu non-Brahmin movement founded by Periyar in 1925, distinct from Ambedkar's separate Mahar / Dalit movements in Maharashtra.

distractor_analysis.reason: Ambedkar led Mahar/Dalit rights movements (Mahad Satyagraha 1927, Independent Labour Party, Republican Party) — separate stream, separate region, NOT Self-Respect Movement.
Bhaskarrao Jadhav was a Satyashodhak Samaj associate (Maharashtra non-Brahmin movement, Phule lineage) — adjacent ideology but different organisation.
Dinkarrao Javalkar (Maharashtra) wrote 'Deshache Dushman'; Satyashodhak/non-Brahmin lineage but not the founder of the Self-Respect Movement.

answer_justification.fact: E.V. Ramasamy Naicker ('Periyar') founded the Self-Respect Movement in 1925 in Tamil Nadu — anti-caste, anti-Brahminical, championed Tamil non-Brahmin identity.
answer_justification.hook: Periyar broke from the Indian National Congress over caste; the movement later became the Dravidar Kazhagam political force.
answer_justification.elimination_path: Recognise that 'Self-Respect Movement' is a SPECIFIC named Tamil Nadu movement (1925, Periyar), not a generic anti-caste movement. Once that pattern fires, A is the only option from Tamil Nadu — eliminate B (Maharashtra/Dalit), C and D (Maharashtra/Satyashodhak).
